searchText: <dcposch> I did some digging. 7212 (both EIP and RIP) originally specified a 32byte return value. Implementations differed, some returning *empty data* for invalid signatures. This is now live on Polygon. The spec was updated retroactively to match the deployed implementation. It's not a huge deal, but it is unfortunate, since it means there can't be a clean fallback: (invalid signature) is now indistinguishable from (7212 not deployed). In both cases, you get a successful call returning no data. Lastly, (mark Final) > (deploy to mainnet) > (retroactively update spec) is a bad precedent for the very first RIP. This is not a criticism of Ulas/Clave—congratulations on getting it to the finish line—but I think the RIP process could use improvement. excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<dcposch> I did some digging.

7212 (both EIP and RIP) originally specified a 32byte return value. Implementations differed, some returning *empty data* for invalid signatures. This is now live on Polygon. The spec was updated retroactively to match the deployed implementation.

It's not a huge deal, but it is unfortunate, since it means there can't be a clean fallback: (invalid signature) is now indistinguishable from (7212 not deployed). In both cases, you get a successful call returning no data.

Lastly, (mark Final) > (deploy to mainnet) > (retroactively update spec) is a bad precedent for the very first RIP.

This is not a criticism of Ulas/Clave—congratulations on getting it to the finish line—but I think the RIP process could use improvement.

Details here:
https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eip-7212-precompiled-for-secp256r1-curve-support/14789/96 (re @ulerdogan: The spec has not changed, just changed to address misunderstandings. It's aligned with chain implementation.)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<dcposch> I don't think it's been changed retroactively to adapt Polygon.
in March we were told to never return 0 in any case (i.e. either empty result or bytes32(1))
I understand this was decided earlier and discussed on RollCalls, but it wasn't actually updated in the RIP until April 25. I linked to the PR.

It's OK--it's shipped, and I don't think it's worth changing.

The lack of clean fallback is not disastrous because luckily, fallback is still possible in the common case: a _valid_ signature can be verified by precompile > fallback to EVM smoothly on non-7212 chains. The problem just renders the precompile moot for _invalid_ signatures, which are rarely onchain. It's also not a security issue, as far as I can tell.

I do think it's worth coming up with a better process going forward.

I'd like to see future RIPs have a machine-readable spec or test of some kind that client implementations can be validated against. Curious to hear people's ideas.

<rjected> I mean, sort of? No new "spec infrastructure" needs to be created is my main point - authors of RIPs / EIPs should focus on writing quality and creating comprehensive test vectors that do things like:
* test important spec details, for example any detail that would warrant a `NB: ` comment
* test edge cases
* common cases, etc.
* or even a reference implementation (this is eels essentially)

once this bar is met for existing specs, then maybe ppl can start thinking about more complex tools
